data.title: Antimony Resources Produces Concentrate Sample from Tecomatlán Proof-of-Concept Campaign
data.description:
An ongoing proof-of-concept campaign at Antimony Resources’ Tecomatlán processing plant in Mexico has produced an estimated 20 tonnes of antimony concentrate to date using an initial feed parcel from the nearby Chinantla mine.

The campaign is generating operating data on throughput, recovery, concentrate quality, and handling to inform the design and economics of an integrated gravity and flotation facility.

The plant’s unitary flotation cells recovered higher-grade material early in the flotation process while the remaining material returned to the main flotation circuit for further recovery, allowing the plant to produce higher grades for blending.

Intermediate concentrate samples from the first three cells assayed up to 65.96% antimony and sampling at different points in the circuit allowed the team to assess the performance of individual stages and use those results to guide operating adjustments.

Concentrate sampled at the unitary flotation stage graded between 55.74% and 65.96% antimony across four November runs, while final samples graded between 22.84% and 56.25%.

In-House Cell Design

One of the most significant improvements to the Tecomatlán flotation circuit has been the integration of hybrid-type flotation cells designed and fabricated in-house to maximise the initial recovery of high-grade antimony concentrate.

The configuration operates in a similar way to a flash flotation circuit, targeting the early recovery of liberated stibnite particles and producing a high-grade concentrate before the material passes through the conventional flotation stages to produce a lower-grade material.

This is expected to improve flotation selectivity, allow for the production of differentiated concentrate grades and potentially enhance overall antimony recovery and concentrate quality.

Tecomatlán’s existing flotation cells remain in the circuit as part of the scavenger and cleaning stages.

Antimony Resources aims for the plant to eventually serve as a regional processing hub for third-party feed, with ore from the Los Lirios project being earmarked as a potential source of company-controlled feed.

Refining Operations

Executive chair Shane Menere said the company was encouraged by the proof-of-concept results.

“Reprocessing concentrate through the circuit over several passes has helped us refine how we operate the plant to output a higher-grade concentrate,” he said.

“The unitary flotation cells we built and installed on site have played an important role by recovering higher-grade material early in the circuit and we are now continuing to refine flotation settings and concentrate handling so we can produce a more consistent product.”

“The progress we have made puts us in a good position to move towards our first commercial sale—our immediate focus is to build inventory, confirm the quality of the finished concentrate and qualify an initial parcel against buyer specifications.”

data.title: US stock futures edge higher after Nvidia surge sparks AI trade rebound
data.description:
US stock futures are slightly higher after Jensen Huang returned as Nvidia CEO sending the chipmaker's shares surging, which sparked a rebound in the AI trade.

The Nasdaq 100 futures were up marginally, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 91 points, or 0.2% and S&P 500 futures increased 0.2%.

Nvidia shares surged 31% in Monday's trading session, leading to a rally in chip stocks. The Nasdaq Composite ended 6.5% up, the S&P 500 closed 4.7% higher while the Dow Industrials gained 3% on Monday.

This was the best session for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq since April 9 last year when the US President Donald Trump had announced a reprieve on tariffs.

The tech sector of the S&P 500 surged 9%, powered by sharp rises in semiconductors, memory and necolouds names. Advanced Micro Devices shares surged almost 7%, while Micron Technology soared 19%. The neocloud stock CoreWeave increased 22%.

Monday's market action was a sharp reversal from the previous trade session on Friday which witnessed a steep sell-off, when the S&P 500 and Dow had ended in correction as the AI trade suffered and Nvidia shares tanked.

data.title: Why Amazon's Rival to Starlink Is Struggling to Catch Up With SpaceX — WSJ
data.description:
By Isabella Simonetti and Drew FitzGerald

Amazon.com is trying to build a satellite-internet business to rival Elon Musk's Starlink. It is struggling to get off the launchpad.

The company has faced a series of setbacks as it races to roll out commercial service by year-end, including a vehicle failure earlier this month. It suffered another small hiccup Monday when rocket company Arianespace briefly delayed a launch of 36 satellites. Amazon is still on track to meet its goal, a company spokesperson said.

Amazon Leo's mission is to provide high-speed internet to remote places using a network of thousands of satellites. SpaceX's Starlink has been doing that for years, but with recent controversy over its activity in Ukraine, governments and consumers are eager for another option.

Amazon's biggest hurdle now is activating the satellites it has already built. The company plans to eventually field thousands of low-Earth-orbit satellites, but getting them into space has been a challenge.

Launch woes

Amazon Leo, which began as "Project Kuiper," received Federal Communications Commission authorization in 2020. It has almost 400 satellites in orbit, while Starlink has more than 11,000, according to the companies.

While Starlink has its own SpaceX vehicles to launch satellites, Amazon relies on a mix of third-party providers, including Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin. The May explosion of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket delayed the launch of Amazon Leo satellites, while its 40-satellite launch using United Launch Alliance's Vulcan vehicle failed earlier this month.

"Amazon seems to have been able to produce these satellites at scale and they're backing up in a warehouse," said Clayton Swope, the deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a think tank.

Swope, who formerly worked on the Amazon satellite project, compared the launch-vehicle bottleneck to the frustration of a ride-share on a busy day. "I'm waiting 30 minutes for an Uber. I don't have a ride to get to where I'm going," he said.

Amazon works with a variety of launch providers, including SpaceX, which it says reduces the risk of depending on a single rocket. It said it has moved up several missions with SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket.

Washington officials have helped clear a path for the new satellite network. The FCC in June waived a requirement that Amazon have more than 1,600 satellites in orbit by the summer. Meanwhile, Commerce Department policies have encouraged states to steer some federal broadband grants to both Starlink and Leo, rather than just to traditional fiber-optic cable companies.

The Commerce Department said the administration's broadband policies support innovation and avoid picking favorites among internet technologies.

High-cost operation

Amazon, America's largest company by annual revenue, is one of the few companies with the financial heft to try to build a satellite fleet.

Each satellite costs Amazon $2 million and the company is spending at least $4 billion on Leo this year, according to Mark Mahaney of Evercore ISI. Amazon declined to comment on the estimates.

"Doing stuff in space at scale is expensive — doing a broadband constellation in space at scale is particularly expensive," Swope said, citing the high manufacturing and launch costs.

Starlink worries

In October, The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk ordered a slowdown of a military-grade version of his Starlink service that Ukraine relies on to target Moscow's military and defend against Russian missile and drone barrages. The disruptions reignited a debate over the geopolitical consequences of SpaceX wielding a near-monopoly over a vital military technology.

"The industry is desperate to have a counterweight to SpaceX," said Chris Quilty, an analyst and partner at research and advisory firm Quilty Space.

Musk has said that the U.S., rather than SpaceX, controls a government version of his satellite service called Starshield.

He said at the New York Times DealBook Summit last week that the company has denied Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's requests to use Starlink's commercial satellites for offensive military actions. When asked about Zelensky's claim that Starshield was slowed down, Musk said, "That's false."

After the interview, Zelensky told CNN, "When I said that Starshield doesn't work, it was 100% truth."

What's next for Amazon Leo

Amazon has a lot riding on its year-end goal for launching commercial service.

Its deal to buy satellite operator Globalstar, announced earlier this year, is part of its effort to link consumer smartphones with satellite internet connections.

Amazon has also signed agreements to provide in-flight Wi-Fi to Delta and JetBlue. Delta Chief Executive Ed Bastian told Bloomberg recently that he was confident in his decision to not choose Starlink, saying the airline plays "the long game."

After the Vulcan launch failure earlier this month, Musk posted a photo on X of a skeleton, writing, "I found a pic of 'the long game.'"

data.title: Macquarie Led Group to Buy Axiata's International Towers in $1.2 Billion Deal
data.description:
By P.R. Venkat

A Macquarie-led consortium has agreed to acquire Axiata's international telecom tower businesses, valued at about $1.2 billion, expanding the Australian asset manager's Southeast Asian digital infrastructure footprint.

The consortium will buy the tower businesses of Malaysian telecom group Axiata's unit Edotco in the Philippines, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Cambodia, Macquarie said Monday.

Its Macquarie Asia-Pacific Infrastructure Fund 4 will acquire the Philippine business, which has about 3,200 towers, while other consortium members will buy the rest.

"The investment reflects our conviction in the continued growth of digital infrastructure across Southeast Asia," said Verena Lim, Asia chief executive of Macquarie Group and co-head of Asia-Pacific infrastructure at Macquarie Asset Management.

In a regulatory filing, PT Tower Bersama Infrastructure said it agreed to buy all of Edotco's Indonesian business. Bangladesh-focused private equity firm Osiris Group said it would buy a 70% stake in the Bangladesh business and all of the Pakistan business.

Malaysia's OCK Group said in a filing that it agreed to buy the Cambodia business, which operates more than 3,800 telecom towers.

In its home market, Axiata will also sell about 15.645% of Edotco Malaysia to state fund Khazanah Nasional for about 659.4 million ringgit, equivalent to $159.9 million. Following the deal Axiata and Khazanah Nasional will each have a 47.355% stake and joint control of the Malaysian business.

The sales are part of a wider restructuring by Axiata that values Edotco at 11.8 billion ringgit.

Axiata expects gross proceeds of about 2.2 billion ringgit, which will mainly be used to pare down debt. The deals are expected to cut its gearing, a measure of debt against equity, to 0.50 times from 0.71 times.

"Reducing leverage and strengthening our balance sheet will give us greater financial and strategic flexibility," Axiata Chief Executive Nik Rizal Kamil said.

The deals need approval from shareholders and regulators. Macquarie expects its purchase to be completed in 2027.

data.title: Forrester: More Than Two-Thirds Of Consumers Expect Their Banking App To Manage All Financial Tasks
data.description:
CommBank, Intesa Sanpaolo, IDFC FIRST Bank, and U.S. Bank lead Forrester's 2026 mobile banking review in Australia, Europe, India, and North America, respectively

SYDNEY, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- According to the Forrester report, The Forrester Digital Experience Review™: Global Mobile Banking Apps, 2026, more than two-thirds of online adults in metro India (82%), Australia (71%), Europe (68%), and the US (67%) expect their mobile banking app to serve as a one-stop destination for managing all their financial tasks; in Canada, 65% of online adults expect the same. Despite these rising expectations, banks are largely making incremental improvements to individual capabilities, including payments, virtual cards, and international transfers, rather than reimagining the entire mobile experience.

The research evaluated the smartphone apps of 22 banks globally. Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CommBank), Intesa Sanpaolo, IDFC FIRST Bank, and U.S. Bank lead in Australia, Europe, India, and North America, respectively. The high-performing banks go beyond everyday transactions, giving customers more control over their finances and helping them manage increasingly complex financial needs within the app.

Key highlights that set global high-performing banks apart:

  • CommBank, the leader in Australia, combines strong self-service with budgeting and investment experiences that help customers make more informed financial decisions. Its app provides starter budgets based on customers' average spending and brings personalized spending insights, investment education, product comparison, account opening, and portfolio management together in the same mobile experience. CommBank overtakes Westpac, which had led the Australian mobile Digital Experience Review for the previous three consecutive years.
  • Intesa Sanpaolo, the highest-performing bank in Europe, gives customers extensive control over complex tasks such as managing loans and mortgages and making international transfers through its app. It also embeds safeguards to help prevent costly mistakes, including flagging potential duplicate transfers and alerting customers to decisions that could result in additional charges.
  • IDFC FIRST Bank, the top-ranking bank in India, provides customers a central hub for managing their finances. Customers can bring together accounts and loans held across different institutions and track their net worth, cash flow, savings goals, and investments in one place. The bank also combines extensive digital self-service with its AI tool, which enables customers to ask questions, retrieve financial information, and complete banking tasks.
  • U.S. Bank, the leading bank in North America, delivers forward-looking financial guidance to help customers respond to emerging needs and automate progress toward their goals. The app includes features such as a money tracker and balance forecast to help customers understand income, spending, and potential future cash-flow pressures, while the app's savings tools enable customers to automate transfers based on their balance, card purchases, or paychecks.

"Consumers increasingly expect their banking app to help them manage their broader financial lives, and the leaders in our review stand out by turning financial insights into action and making everyday tasks simpler," said Zhi-Ying Barry, principal analyst at Forrester and lead author of the report. "As AI models learn to handle complex, multistep goals, banks need to decide how much of that journey they want to own and how much they'll cede to third-party agents."

About Forrester

Forrester (Nasdaq: FORR) is one of the most influential research and advisory firms in the world. We empower leaders in technology, customer experience, digital, marketing, revenue, and product functions to make confident decisions in an AI-driven world and accelerate growth through customer obsession. Our unique research and continuous guidance model helps executives and their teams achieve their initiatives and outcomes faster and with confidence. To learn more, visit Forrester.com.

data.title: Agoda and GSTC Deliver Thailand's First Accessibility and Inclusion in Hospitality Training
data.description:
BANGKOK, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Digital travel platform Agoda and the Global Sustainable Tourism Council (GSTC) delivered Thailand's first GSTC Accessibility & Inclusion in Hospitality Training on 23 November at Agoda's One Bangkok office. Held ahead of the International Day of Persons with Disabilities on 3 December, the full-day program brought together over 70 hospitality professionals from Bangkok and nearby provinces to explore practical ways to make travel experiences more accessible and inclusive.

The session marked the first GSTC accessibility training delivered in partnership with an online travel platform. It extends Agoda's Sustainable Tourism Academy, an ongoing initiative through which Agoda is the first global online travel platform to partner with GSTC on sustainability training for accommodation partners. To date, the Academy has reached more than 5,200 hospitality professionals and aspiring professionals through in-person sessions and a digital learning platform.

The program was endorsed by the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration (BMA) and opened with a keynote address from Bangkok Governor Chadchart Sittipunt, who noted that accessibility cannot be achieved by the government alone and requires collaboration among government, businesses, communities and people with lived experience. He added that initiatives like this show how public-private partnerships can accelerate that progress.

There is a clear case for improved accessibility. According to the World Health Organization, approximately one in six people worldwide live with a disability, and UN Tourism estimates the potential accessible travel market in Asia Pacific at 690 million people. This latent demand shows up in traveler behavior: a 2025 Korea Tourism Organization survey found that 93% of travelers with accessibility needs would travel more often if barriers were removed, and 76% would pay more for better options.

The training was designed to help hospitality teams act on that opportunity. With costs covered by Agoda, trainer-led sessions covered accessibility standards and frameworks, market trends, the business case for inclusion and practical hospitality approaches. Participants also took part in role-plays, games and a group exercise focused on addressing accessibility challenges from different hospitality perspectives. Attendees represented hostels, independent hotels and hotel groups, including Six Senses, Dusit and Minor, in roles spanning ownership, general management, sustainability, learning and development, and marketing.

Andrew Smith, Senior Vice President, Supply at Agoda, said, "Accessibility decides whether a traveler can plan a trip with confidence and feel welcome once they arrive. Most of that comes down to details a hotel team can fix if they know what to look for. Working with GSTC, we're bringing hospitality teams together to turn that into practical steps they can use."

Randy Durband, CEO of GSTC, added, "Accessibility is a core part of sustainable tourism. A destination can't be truly sustainable if it isn't open to everyone. We're pleased to bring this training to Thailand with Agoda and give hospitality professionals practical tools to welcome guests of all abilities."

Beyond the training, Agoda is continuously working to improve the accessibility of its website and mobile apps, striving to deliver inclusive digital experiences for all users. This includes working on compatibility with assistive technologies, keyboard navigation, support for users' text-size preferences, and implementing a dedicated feedback form for reporting accessibility issues on our platform. These efforts are supported by accessibility training, research with people with disabilities, and ongoing testing, audits, and remediation.

SOURCE Agoda

data.title: Trump orders US Army to pause detonation of lead explosives in Iowa
data.description:
Key points:
  • US appeals court lifts previous stay that blocked detonation
  • Trump wants both court and governor-elect to OK demolition plan
  • Opponents raise concerns about toxic lead dust cloud

By Renee Hickman and Steve Gorman

US President Donald Trump ordered the Army on Monday to hold off on its plan to blow up a deteriorating stockpile of toxic lead explosives in rural Iowa, saying it should be up to the courts and the state's governor-elect to decide whether to allow the detonation.

Hours later, the 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals gave judicial clearance for the detonation plan, lifting a stay the court issued Thursday temporarily freezing an Environmental Protection Agency permit for the demolition.

But the immediate status of the plan remained unclear.

The Army stirred a public outcry last week when details surfaced of its plan to detonate 68 storage drums, or nearly 10,000 pounds (4,500 kilograms), of degraded lead azide, an explosive chemical used in military munitions, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa.

Environmental groups challenging the Army's disposal plan in court have raised public safety concerns over the likelihood that the explosion would release a plume of toxic lead dust over homes, crops and livestock far beyond the detonation site.

The EPA has countered that a managed detonation would be far less risky than an uncontrolled, spontaneous explosion of the dangerously unstable material, a scenario the agency said was growing more likely as the weather turns colder in Iowa. According to the EPA, any attempt to relocate the storage drums would likewise risk spontaneous explosion.

Writing on his Truth Social platform on Monday, Trump said he believed "the proper course" was for the Army to proceed with the controlled detonation. But the Republican president added that he has "ordered the military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward."

He also said Iowa's Democratic governor-elect, Rob Sand, should approve any such decision. Sand does not take office until January so lacks authority to act until then.

'NO GOOD OPTIONS EXIST'

Sand posted a statement on X kicking the issue back to Trump, saying, "The Administration should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks."

The governor-elect wrote on Sunday that "no good options exist" and called for "transparency over how we got here."

The current governor, Republican Kim Reynolds, on Sunday said she had activated Iowa's emergency operations center to better coordinate between state and federal agencies, including the Army, EPA and US Department of Agriculture.

“While the detonation is a federal operation, it’s important for the state to be engaged in the preparation process so we can support the work of our federal partners in responding to the needs of Iowans,” Reynolds said. “Protecting the health and safety of our people and communities is our highest priority.”

Trump's statement appeared to reverse the government's position on Saturday, when its lawyers told the court the Army planned to proceed under an emergency exemption to federal environmental laws.

Although Monday's ruling removed the final legal obstacle, it remained unclear whether the Army would move forward after Trump said the governor-elect should also agree.

Trump wrote that if the Army did not proceed and an accident later occurred, Sand would bear responsibility.

data.title: Elon Musk Warns AI Firms Could Face a Cash Crisis in 2027
data.description:
Elon Musk warned AI firms could face a cash crisis in 2027, saying delays in bringing hardware online could require hundreds of billions of dollars in extra working capital. Lenders priced roughly $44 billion in debt to finance AI chips for SpaceX a day earlier, according to BeInCrypto; the chips are due in the first half of 2027, with payments starting on delivery, potentially months before they generate revenue.

SpaceX reported $13.1 billion in operating cash flow and $48.1 billion in capital expenditure during the first nine months of 2026, resulting in $35 billion of negative free cash flow. It holds nearly $90 billion in cash and marketable securities, while its AI division generated $7.56 billion in third-quarter revenue; Starlink and rocket launches provide additional income. The largest portion of the chip financing carries an 8.259% yield, Reuters reported.

Musk predicted widespread failures among more than 200 AI-computing providers, or neoclouds, in October and later ruled out SpaceX acquiring them. The warning comes amid weaker investor confidence: the S&P 500 fell 2% during last week’s Anthropic IPO selloff, and 20 major technology stocks entered bear market territory. The article cites roughly $1 trillion in telecom debt before the early-2000s industry collapse as a precedent, and says the key question for AI companies is whether revenue can cover infrastructure costs.

data.title: StarHub-M1 deal to create Singapore telecoms group with $3.9 billion enterprise value
data.description:
Singaporean telecoms firm StarHub said on Tuesday it had agreed to acquire mobile operator M1, majority-owned by Keppel , in an all-stock deal that will create a combined entity with an enterprise value of S$5 billion ($3.87 billion).

StarHub will issue 651.7 million shares to fund the acquisition, representing about 27.4% of the enlarged share capital.

Upon closing, M1 will become a StarHub unit, with asset manager Keppel holding an effective 23% stake in the combined entity. M1's other shareholders will receive the balance of the newly issued shares.

As of Tuesday, Keppel owns an effective interest of about 83.9% in M1.

This follows an earlier failed attempt by Australia-listed Tuas to buy Keppel's stake in M1 for S$1.43 billion after the Singaporean regulator suspended its review of the transaction.

($1 = 1.2922 Singapore dollars)

data.title: Gold edges up on bargain buying after selloff; US inflation data awaited
data.description:
Gold prices rose slightly on Tuesday, extending a rebound from a 14-month low as bargain hunters returned after last week's sharp selloff, with investors awaiting US inflation data for fresh signals on the Federal Reserve's interest-rate outlook.

FUNDAMENTALS

* Spot gold rose 0.4% to $3,645.29 per ounce by 0023 GMT, while US gold futures for December delivery fell 0.2% to $3,644.70.

* New York Fed President John Williams said on Monday that persistently high inflation continues to point the US central bank towards tighter monetary policy, while stressing that the pace of future rate hikes will depend on incoming economic data.

* The US Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Index, a key gauge closely watched by the central bank as it targets a 2% inflation rate, is due on Wednesday.

* Markets are pricing in a 95% chance of a 25-basis-point rate increase at the Fed's policy meeting in December, while a larger 50-bp hike is priced in at 4.9%, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

* Higher interest rates increase the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion, reducing its appeal to investors.

* US stocks soared on Monday after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO following pressure from US President Donald Trump.

* A European Central Bank rate hike next month may not be enough to fully contain inflation but a follow-up move is not urgent given that worrisome second-round effects are building only gradually, Lithuanian policymaker Gediminas Simkus said.

data.title: Space sector needs a manufacturing boost
data.description:
On July 18, 2026, Skyroot’s Vikram-1 lifted off and reached orbit. It became India’s first privately built orbital launch. What mattered was not the launch itself but the distinction it proved: that an Indian company could design, engineer and manufacture a sophisticated launch vehicle using indigenous capability, not assembled capability bought in from elsewhere.

This distinction is the one India’s space ambitions will rest on. Propulsion assemblies, turbo-machinery, composite structures, flight computers and inertial navigation units must perform within extremely narrow tolerance windows, repeatedly, without the margin for error that most industries allow. A country that depends on external suppliers for these components cannot claim genuine technological sovereignty, however well it integrates the final product. Many of Skyroot’s founding engineers, like much of the private space sector’s senior bench, were trained inside the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) before building a company of their own. A lineage worth remembering, even as these companies build manufacturing depth beyond ISRO.

A market too large

The opportunity is real. India’s space economy is about $8.4 billion, with IN-SPACe targeting $44 billion over the next decade. This is inside a global space economy McKinsey projects could expand from $630 billion to $1.8 trillion by 2035. The more consequential shift lies downstream. Applications that depend on space-based connectivity and data are expected to grow from $300 billion to over a trillion dollars by 2035. Space infrastructure is becoming the invisible layer beneath precision agriculture, logistics, energy, disaster response and financial services.

India now has over 450 space startups. The funded ones have together raised $871 million, a number read everywhere as proof of momentum. It is better read as a question. What is this capital building: qualified component suppliers, repeatable manufacturing processes, testing facilities that certify a satellite part to international standard, or merely more companies chasing the same unproven supply chain?

This is a Schumpeterian moment in the fullest sense. The 2025 economics Nobel honoured both creative destruction and the prerequisites for sustained growth.

Reusable launch vehicles, miniaturised electronics and cheaper access to orbit are not only improving the existing satellite business; they are making its old economics obsolete, the way creative destruction always does. Beneath that shorter cycle runs a longer one. Space-based connectivity, navigation and sensing are becoming integral to ordinary economic activity. That is the signature of a new Kondratiev wave, the kind of general-purpose infrastructure shift that reorganises how entire economies produce. Global capital has already priced this in. SpaceX’s record-setting IPO this June, valuing the company close to $1.8 trillion, shows where investors expect value to accumulate.

Capital follows capability

Manufacturing competence, not capital, will decide the outcome, because capital alone cannot buy what manufacturing competence takes decades to build. Precision-produced satellites, reusable propulsion, advanced materials and sophisticated onboard electronics depend on accumulated engineering depth: additive manufacturing for complex geometries, materials science that survives repeated thermal and vibration stress, qualification regimes that reject a batch for a single reading out of specification. A design remains theoretical until every component has withstood the extreme stresses of launch, spaceflight and years of operating life. That is why high-end manufacturing is not the final stage after invention but part of the invention process itself.

India has built real institutional foundations for this: ISRO’s accumulated technological depth, IN-SPACe as a facilitator of private participation, NSIL as the commercialisation interface and a growing bench of private manufacturers and research institutions. What has been missing, until recently, is the mechanism that connects them.

A recent ₹1,200-crore public-private project offers an early sign of it. Under it, a Pixxel-led consortium of four startups will build and operate India’s first indigenous Earth-observation satellite constellation, sharing risk, pooling component supply and building a path from publicly funded research to industrial-scale production.

Building a tiered domestic supplier base for propulsion, electronics and precision subsystems will need more such projects, plus shared testing and qualification infrastructure open to the whole sector, not just one consortium.

International competition will not wait for India to build it. European space startups have raised a record $3.9 billion so far this year, according to Dealroom. $1.1 billion of it went to Finland’s ICEYE, which has carved a defensible position in synthetic-aperture radar earth observation on the strength of specialised engineering and manufacturing capability, not market size or state backing. China and Japan are both accelerating public investment in domestic launch capacity. None of these countries are winning on enthusiasm or talent pipelines alone. They are winning on manufacturing capacity that already exists and can be deployed the moment capital arrives.

SCALE is the enabler

None of this is possible without the right engineering workforce. This is where SCALE (Skills, Capability, Agility, Learning and Entrepreneurship) belongs. But SCALE enables; it does not found. Engineers trained for mathematical reasoning, systems thinking and challenge-based design are necessary; they are not sufficient on their own to manufacture a qualified turbo-pump or a flight computer that survives vibration testing.

That capability has to already exist as a platform before an agile, well-trained graduate has anything real to build on.

ISRO built such a platform slowly, over four decades of mission assurance, with no commercial pressure to compromise it. Manufacturing discipline is the foundation; SCALE and capital are the enablers that act on it, not substitutes for it. Neglect that foundation and India produces graduates fluent in systems thinking and design software, able to sketch a turbo-pump beautifully, who have never had to qualify one against a specification that forgives nothing.

India’s space leadership will not be decided by the frequency of its technological breakthroughs.

It will be decided by whether those breakthroughs can be manufactured reliably, qualified rigorously and reproduced economically, launch after launch, without the fanfare a first flight earns. Entrepreneurial energy and venture capital can accelerate this transition but cannot substitute for it. Vikram-1 proved Indian engineering can do this once.

The task now is to institutionalise the conversion of scientific research into repeatable manufacturing capability, so that what Vikram-1 achieved becomes routine rather than exceptional.

Technological sovereignty is capability on demand, not capability by circumstance.

Sondhi is former MD and CEO, Ashok Leyland and JCB India; Verma, Professor IIT Kanpur, is former Secretary, Science and Engineering Research Board, Government of India.

data.title: Ethereum Foundation doubles protocol security team ahead of overhaul
data.description:
The Ethereum Foundation says it has doubled its protocol security team as it accelerates work to overhaul Ethereum’s defenses against threats posed by quantum computers and artificial intelligence.

In a Monday blog post, Ethereum Foundation researcher Kev Wedderburn said that while Ethereum has been planning ways to mitigate threats posed by quantum computers, AI has now emerged as a more urgent risk.

The planned overhaul would change how Ethereum validators sign messages, how users authorize transactions and how Ethereum verifies data posted by rollups.

“This upgrade is harder than the Merge, and we have less time,” said Wedderburn, while acknowledging that faster development “makes it easier to ship bugs.”

He said in response, the foundation has expanded its protocol security team to ensure formal verification and security work can keep pace with development.

“Every layer of the protocol and ecosystem will need to adapt to the reality that hardening the protocol is now our highest priority,” he added.

Earlier this month, Ethereum Foundation researcher Justin Drake outlined a December 2028 target for completing Ethereum’s post-quantum and post-AI transition, a year earlier than the foundation’s previously announced quantum-resistance deadline.

data.title: Bank of Korea Set to Raise Rate This Week, Poll Says — Market Talk
data.description: The Bank of Korea is expected to raise its base rate by 25 bps to 3.25% at its policy meeting Thursday. Of 25 analysts surveyed by The Wall Street Journal, 23 expect a quarter-percentage-point rate increase in November after the BOK held steady in October. Some expect the BOK to revise up its growth and inflation forecasts for 2026 and 2027, as demand for chips used in artificial intelligence boosts exports and price pressure persist. Inflation remains above the 2% target, with both headline and core consumer prices rising 2.8% on year in October, while robust semiconductor exports continue to underpin growth, ING economists Deepali Bhargava and Lynn Song say in a note.(kwanwoo.jun@wsj.com)

data.title: CFTC staff say bitcoin, ether can count toward derivatives firms’ operating expenses
data.description:
Staff at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission issued an advisory saying certain regulated clearinghouses and exchanges may count cryptocurrencies such as bitcoin and ether toward a requirement to maintain enough assets to cover at least one year of operating expenses.

On Monday, the agency's Division of Market Oversight and Division of Clearing and Risk released that advisory and said ether, bitcoin, and payment stablecoins could be counted toward that requirement — and would be subject to a haircut — a regulatory discount applied to their market value to account for potential losses.

"Pleased to see @CFTC staff continue to provide important clarity around crypto assets in US derivatives markets through today’s staff advisory," said CFTC Chair Michael Selig in a post on X.

The advisory applies to swap execution facilities, clearing organizations and designated contract markets. It also does not create new legal obligations and is not enforceable. The CFTC also noted that crypto do not qualify as cash or very liquid securities under the Generally Accepted Accounting Principles — the set of accounting rules used by U.S. companies to report financial statements — so they are not eligible towards a liquidity requirement, which is separate.

Katherine Kirkpatrick Bos, Chainlink Labs' head of legal, called the advisory "significant."

"People don't realize that one of the impediments to these licenses is the cost of holding a lot of $ - this will help," she said in a post on X.

Also on Monday, the CFTC published its final rule creating a reporting framework for certain event contracts. Rulemaking was necessary, the CFTC said, because the agency had previously moved through a no-action letter process and those don't carry the "force of law," and it also wanted to standardize reported data.

The final rule adds a new part regarding clarifying dates for compliance.

“The CFTC will no longer regulate market participants through a patchwork of no-action letters, which serve as band-aids for unworkable regulations," Selig said in a statement. "This final rule is an important step in future-proofing the regulatory framework for event contracts."

data.title: What are the various US federal and state probes faced by Nvidia and Jensen Huang?
data.description:
By Kanishka Singh

As President Donald Trump welcomed Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO and declared the tech billionaire's return posed no national security risk, the company and its boss faced a host of state and federal probes and reviews.

Here are details on some of those actions, with their status in certain cases remaining unclear:

FBI AND US INTELLIGENCE REVIEWS:

After reports that the Nvidia CEO had an extramarital affair with unrelated Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whom US intelligence agencies probed over whether she was a Chinese asset, Trump said on November 9 the FBI was "looking into" the issue.

Jensen Huang has acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and apologized, but has not ​publicly addressed the situation further. China has denied the espionage allegations.

US intelligence agencies examined the extent of the Chinese businesswoman's ties to China's Ministry of State Security and what information she may have passed to Beijing, people familiar with the matter have told Reuters.

When asked after the Nvidia CEO's reinstatement what the CIA had told Trump, the president told CNBC: "Let me just say, I have clearance. And if I didn't have clearance, I wouldn't have done ​the deal (with Nvidia's board for Jensen Huang's return)."

Trump said Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed the federal government has no evidence that Huang engaged in unlawful conduct.

The New York Times reported that Alice Huang kept in contact with an official from China's top spy agency for more than a year during the affair. China's foreign ministry has previously said the spy accusations were "groundless," and Reuters has been unable to determine Alice Huang's whereabouts to seek comment.

Nvidia's board has formed a committee to investigate ​whether foreign intelligence efforts targeted Jensen Huang and is also starting a search to name a new chief compliance officer.

ANTITRUST PROBE:

The Justice Department has also been reviewing Nvidia's $12.9 billion deal to buy open-source platform Hugging Face alongside a broader antitrust investigation into the company's acquisitions and practices, Reuters reported in October.

The ‌Justice Department's recent questioning covers Nvidia's acquisitions, investments, sales practices, and whether the chip designer has exerted pressure on its customers, people familiar with the matter said in October.

The Justice Department has also scrutinized Nvidia's ​conduct following other transactions, including ⁠its 2025 deal to license technology from chip startup Groq and hire its engineers, Reuters has reported.

Officials have explored whether Nvidia unfairly offered larger allocations of AI chips if customers purchased its networking equipment and Groq processors, raising questions about whether Nvidia used its dominant product to push into a newer market.

Nvidia, which is a cornerstone ​of the tech economy and AI boom, has declined to comment on the probes.

SEC PROBE:

The US Securities and Exchange Commission is probing Nvidia's accounting practices, Reuters reported on November 20, citing two people briefed on the matter.

Reuters could not immediately determine when the SEC opened its ​inquiry or exactly what potential accounting issues the watchdog examined.

Analysts and investors have grown increasingly concerned about circular AI financing deals, in which chipmakers including Nvidia have pursued complex financial arrangements to help customers fund purchases of their chips and the construction of costly AI infrastructure, such as data centers.

Nvidia has backed AI companies and cloud providers ​and provided guarantees connected to data-center projects that use its equipment. Critics say such arrangements can make it harder for investors to assess ​the quality of chipmakers' revenue ⁠and their true financial exposure.

On its November 17 earnings call, Nvidia's then-interim CEO Colette Kress said the company was proud of its role in supporting the AI industry, but would be far more ⁠selective about future AI industry financing deals.

CALIFORNIA STATE PROBE:

California Attorney General Rob Bonta said on November 19 his office had served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia related to reports of Huang's affair with the Chinese businesswoman.

The probe will help determine whether Nvidia's actions violated California law, the attorney general's office said.

CONGRESSIONAL PROBES:

Democrats, who will hold a majority in the House of Representatives and the Senate from January following the November midterm elections, have been very critical of Huang and Nvidia and of Huang's ties to the Republican president. US ‌lawmakers from both parties sharply criticized Nvidia's decision to reinstate Huang as CEO.

"Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other Nvidia executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain," top Senate Democrat Chuck Schumer said after Huang was reinstated.

Top House Democrat Hakeem Jeffries said Congress will "not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by Nvidia."

Huang has voiced support for Trump's AI agenda and met the Republican leader many times as Nvidia has sought to sell advanced chips to the ‌Chinese market and lobbied for looser restrictions on Chinese access to Nvidia's sophisticated AI chips.

Democratic and Republican lawmakers have called to halt exports of advanced AI chips to China. Huang and the White House have argued that continuing US sales to China would keep Chinese customers reliant on US technology.

Huang has agreed to testify before the US Senate in a public hearing on December 3, the Senate Banking Committee said.

The chairs of the House committees on China, intelligence and foreign affairs separately said Huang and Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter have confirmed they will appear for transcribed interviews on December 1 and December 2 as previously planned.

MEGASPEED PROBES:

Democratic lawmakers have opened a probe into what influence Nvidia was able to wield over a US Commerce Department investigation of Singapore-based cloud-computing company Megaspeed for possible illegal diversion of chips to China, according ‌to a November 19 letter reviewed by Reuters.

The Chinese businesswoman with whom the Nvidia boss had an affair is a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner that operates data centers. Megaspeed said it complies with all applicable laws, including US ⁠export control ​requirements.

Nvidia said that as an American ​company it consults with department officials to answer questions, provide information and request guidance.

The Commerce and ​Justice departments released information on November 16 about Washington's investigation into Megaspeed, Nvidia's Asia-Pacific partner, which the departments said ‌began two years ago.

They said Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia ​in May 2025 about sales to the company and, with Singaporean authorities, conducted an ​on-site inspection in June 2025 at Megaspeed and interviewed Alice Huang.

Washington added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist on November 23.
